The stem shows dark, water-soaked rings where the tissue collapsed, another classic sign of Frost injury. These visible changes are the result of exposure to temperatures below the plant’s 0°C threshold, which killed blossoms and began discoloring the stem. To protect the remaining foliage, apply a 3–4 cm (1.5–1.6 in) layer of floating row cover each evening when forecasts predict 2 °C (36 °F) or lower, ensuring the fabric touches the soil to trap ground heat. Add a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch around the crown to insulate roots and reduce radiant heat loss. Before each sunrise, run a low-flow fan or mist the canopy with 1 L of water per plant, allowing it to dry by mid-morning to prevent further moisture-related damage. Over the next seven days, check each morning for new blackened centers on petals, monitor stem firmness with a gentle tug test, and verify that leaf surfaces remain flat rather than cupped—any deviation signals continuing Frost stress.

attempts.report: The root system of the plant is dark brown and mushy, indicating rot, and the crown tissue shows a black, water-soaked ring at the root-to-stem junction. The root appears shriveled and brittle, with no white feeder roots, a classic sign of decay. These visual cues point to root rot, specifically Phytophthora or Pythium infection that thrives in saturated, poorly aerated media. Immediately remove and discard the affected plant and any nearby soil, then replant in a raised bed or container with a 10-15 cm layer of coarse bark or perlite to improve drainage. Irrigate only when the top 2.5 cm of soil is dry, supplying roughly 250 ml per plant every 3–4 days, ensuring excess water drains within 30 minutes. Add a 1 cm layer of clean straw mulch to moderate moisture without trapping excess water, and maintain 25 cm spacing between plants for airflow. Over the next 7 days, inspect daily for any new blackened, water-soaked roots, check that new leaves remain firm and green rather than wilting, and verify that soil surface dries to the touch between waterings. If any root section turns brown or smells sour, remove it immediately and repeat sanitation steps.

The stem and leaflet are pale green with small, sunken areas where petals used to be, indicating cellular collapse rather than water loss. These discolored, collapsed tissues are the Frost-injured calyx and floral parts, which are the most visible symptoms of the diagnosis. To protect the plant, immediately drape a lightweight floating row cover or fleece over the bed each evening when temperatures are forecast below 2 °C (36 °F), ensuring the fabric is secured to the soil to trap warmth beneath. Add a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch around crowns to reduce radiant heat loss and moderate soil moisture. For each day above 7 °C (45 °F), open the cover for 6–8 hours to allow airflow and prevent overheating. Over the next seven days, check each morning for any new blackened petals or softened flower centers, note any spread of discoloration, and confirm the top 2 cm (¾ in) of soil remains moist but not waterlogged to confirm the protection measures are working.

The most striking feature is a cluster of dark-brown, water-soaked patches on the upper surface of several leaflets, especially the central one. These areas are slightly sunken and have a matte, velvety texture instead of the usual glossy green. The edges of the damaged tissue curl downward, indicating cell collapse from sub-freezing temperatures. The remaining green tissue is still intact but has a pale, yellowish hue at the margins, suggesting limited but uneven chlorophyll loss. These visual cues point to Frost Injury, which freezes and kills epidermal cells, leaving behind necrotic spots. To prevent further damage, immediately cover the plant with a breathable Frost cloth or light blanket, ensuring it is securely draped over the entire crown and at least 10 cm (4 in) off the soil. Add a 5 cm (2 in) layer of clean straw mulch around the base to insulate roots and reduce radiant heat loss. Before the next predicted Frost event, irrigate the soil to a depth of 2 cm (¾ in) in late afternoon to release latent heat overnight, and ensure any overhead watering is suspended until temperatures rise above 0 °C (32 °F). Monitor over the next 7 days for new blackened spots expanding beyond existing borders or wilting that persists longer than 12 h, and repeat protective measures if these signs appear.
